origin.title: Demographics of the Supreme Court of the United States

doc.text:
{{Short description|none}} {{Use mdy dates|date=March 2021}} {{SCOTUS series}} The '''demographics of the Supreme Court of the United States''' encompass the [[gender]], [[ethnicity]], and religious, geographic, and economic backgrounds of the 116 people who have been appointed and confirmed as justices to the [[Supreme Court of the United States|Supreme Court]]. Some of these characteristics have been raised as an issue since the court was established in 1789. For its first 180 years, justices were almost always [[White people|white]] [[Man|male]] [[Protestants]] of [[White Anglo Saxon Protestant|Anglo]] or [[Northwestern Europe]]an descent.{{cite book |last=[[#SegalSpaeth2002|Segal and Spaeth]] |year=2002 |title=The Supreme Court and the Attitudinal Model Revisited|page=183}} Prior to the 20th century, a few [[Catholics]] were appointed, but concerns about diversity on the court were mainly in terms of geographic diversity, to represent all [[Regionalism (politics)|geographic regions]] of the country, as opposed to ethnic, religious, or gender diversity.{{cite book|last=[[#OBrien2003|O'Brien]]|title=Storm Center |year=2003 |page=46}} The 20th century saw the first appointment of justices who were Jewish ([[Louis Brandeis]], 1916), African-American ([[Thurgood Marshall]], 1967), female ([[Sandra Day O'Connor]], 1981), and Italian-American ([[Antonin Scalia]], 1986). The first appointment of a [[Hispanic and Latino Americans|Hispanic]] justice was in the 21st century with [[Sonia Sotomayor]] in 2009, with the possible exception of Justice [[Benjamin Cardozo]], a [[Sephardi Jews|Sephardi Jew]] of [[Portuguese American|Portuguese descent]], who was appointed in 1932. In spite of the interest in the court's demographics and the symbolism accompanying the inevitably political appointment process,{{cite book|last=[[#OBrien2003|O'Brien]] |title=Storm Center |year=2003|page=54}} and the views of some commentators that no demographic considerations should arise in the selection process,{{Cite web|url=http://www.bsos.umd.edu/gvpt/lpbr/subpages/reviews/perry.htm|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20081008010142/http://www.bsos.umd.edu/gvpt/lpbr/subpages/reviews/perry.htm|url-status=dead|title=John P. McIver, Department of Political Science, University of Colorado, Boulder ''Review of A "Representative" Supreme Court? The Impact of Race, Religion, and Gender on Appointments by Barbara A. Perry''.|archivedate=October 8, 2008}}[http://www.grin.com/e-book/37916/appointment-and-nomination-of-supreme-court-justices ''See also'' Kreimendahl, Ilka (2002) ''Appointment and Nomination of Supreme Court Justices'' (Scholarly Paper, Advanced Seminar), ''Amerikanische Entwicklung im Spiegel ausgewählter Entscheidungen des Supreme Court''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090107132324/http://www.grin.com/e-book/37916/appointment-and-nomination-of-supreme-court-justices |date=January 7, 2009 }}, [[University of Kassel]] 32 pages. the gender, race, educational background or religious views of the justices has played little documented role in their jurisprudence. For example, the opinions of the first two African-American justices reflected radically different judicial philosophies; [[William J. Brennan, Jr.|William Brennan]] and [[Antonin Scalia]] shared Catholic faith and a [[Harvard Law School]] education, but shared little in the way of jurisprudential philosophies. The court's first two female justices voted together no more often than with their male colleagues, and historian Thomas R. Marshall writes that no particular "female perspective" can be discerned from their opinions.{{cite book |last=[[#Marshall2008|Marshall]]|title=Public Opinion and the Rehnquist Court|year=2008|page=109}} ==Geographic background== For most of the existence of the court, geographic diversity was a key concern of presidents in choosing justices to appoint. This was prompted in part by the early practice of Supreme Court justices also "riding circuit"—individually hearing cases in different regions of the country. In 1789, the United States was divided into judicial circuits, and from that time until 1891, Supreme Court justices also acted as judges within those individual circuits.{{cite book|last=[[#SegalSpaeth2002|Segal and Spaeth]] |title=The Supreme Court and the Attitudinal Model Revisited |year=2002|page=182}} [[George Washington]] was careful to make appointments "with no two justices serving at the same time hailing from the same state".{{cite book|last=[[#Marshall2008|Marshall]]|title=Public Opinion and the Rehnquist Court|year=2008 |page=108}} [[Abraham Lincoln]] broke with this tradition during the [[American Civil War|Civil War]], and "by the late 1880s presidents disregarded it with increasing frequency".[[#SegalSpaeth2002|Segal and Spaeth]] (2002), quoting Richard Friedman, "The Transformation in Senate Response to Supreme Court Nominations", 5 Cardozo Law Review 1 (1983), p. 50. Although the importance of regionalism declined, it still arose from time to time. For example, in appointing [[Benjamin Cardozo]] in 1929, President Hoover was as concerned about the controversy over having three New York justices on the court as he was about having two Jewish justices.{{cite book|last=[[#SegalSpaeth2002|Segal and Spaeth]]|title=The Supreme Court and the Attitudinal Model Revisited |year=2002|pages=182–83}} David M. O'Brien notes that "from the appointment of [[John Rutledge]] from [[South Carolina]] in 1789 until the retirement of [[Hugo Black]] [from [[Alabama]]] in 1971, with the exception of the [[Reconstruction era of the United States|Reconstruction]] decade of 1866–1876, there was always a southerner on the bench. Until 1867, the sixth seat was reserved as the "southern seat". Until Cardozo's appointment in 1932, the third seat was reserved for [[New England]]ers."{{cite book |last=[[#OBrien2003|O'Brien]] |title=Storm Center|year=2003|pages=46–47}} The westward expansion of the U.S. led to concerns that the western states should be represented on the court as well, which purportedly prompted [[William Howard Taft]] to make his 1910 appointment of [[Willis Van Devanter]] of [[Wyoming]].{{cite book|last=[[#OBrien2003|O'Brien]] |title=Storm Center|year= 2003 |page=47}} Geographic balance was sought in the 1970s, when [[Richard Nixon|Nixon]] attempted to employ a "Southern strategy", hoping to secure support from Southern states by nominating judges from the region. Nixon unsuccessfully nominated Southerners [[Clement Haynsworth]] of [[South Carolina]] and [[G. Harrold Carswell]] of Florida, before finally succeeding with the nomination of [[Harry Blackmun]] of [[Minnesota]].{{cite book|last=[[#OBrien2003|O'Brien]]|title=Storm Center|year=2003 |page=48}} The issue of regional diversity was again raised with the 2010 retirement of [[John Paul Stevens]], who had been appointed from the midwestern Seventh Circuit, leaving the court with all but one Justice having been appointed from states on the East Coast.Mark Sherman, [https://www.nbcnews.com/id/wbna36890869 Is Supreme Court in need of regional diversity?] (May 1, 2010). The majority of justices have come from the Northeastern United States, with most hailing from New York and [[Massachusetts]].{{cite web |last1=Bemis |first1=Tom |title=Supreme Court Justices Historically Come From the Northeast |url=https://www.thestreet.com/politics/supreme-court-justices-historically-come-from-the-northeast-14073809 |website=TheStreet |language=en-us |date=5 April 2017}} 50% of justices have come from just 6 states. Some states have been over-represented, partly because there were fewer states from which early justices could be appointed. New York has produced fifteen justices, three of whom have served as chief justice. [[Ohio]] has produced ten justices, including two chief justices; [[Massachusetts]] nine (including Stephen Breyer and Elena Kagan); and [[Virginia]] eight, including three chief justices. There have been six justices each from [[Pennsylvania]], [[Tennessee]], and [[Maryland]] (the latter including current chief justice John Roberts and current associate justice Brett Kavanaugh); and five each from [[Kentucky]] and [[New Jersey]]. States that have produced four justices include California, Illinois (one chief and three associates each), and [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]] (the third including current associate justice [[Clarence Thomas]]). [[File:DJBrewer.jpg|thumb|upright|[[David J. Brewer]] was born to [[missionary]] parents in [[Smyrna]], in the [[Ottoman Empire]], (now [[İzmir]], [[Turkey]]).]] ===Other states from which justices have been appointed=== * Three justices have been appointed from Connecticut (2 chiefs and 1 associate). * Three justices have been appointed from South Carolina (1 chief, 1 chief who was earlier an associate, and 1 associate). * Three associate justices have been appointed from Alabama. * Two associate justices have been appointed from Colorado, including current associate justice Neil Gorsuch. * Two associate justices have been appointed from Iowa, Indiana, Michigan, Minnesota, North Carolina, and New Hampshire. * One associate justice has been appointed from Arizona, while another associate justice who later became chief was born there had moved to Virginia prior to their appointment. * One justice, who served both as an associate and as chief, has been appointed from Louisiana; current associate justice Amy Coney Barrett was born and raised there, but had moved to Indiana prior to her appointment. * One associate justice has been appointed from Kansas, Maine, Missouri, Mississippi, Texas, Utah, and Wyoming.{{cite web |title=Justices 1789 to Present |url=https://www.supremecourt.gov/about/members_text.aspx |website=www.supremecourt.gov}} ===States from which no justices have been appointed=== Despite the efforts to achieve geographic balance, only seven justices{{efn|[[David J. Brewer]] from Kansas; [[Byron White]] and [[Neil Gorsuch]] from Colorado; [[Willis Van Devanter]] from Wyoming; [[George Sutherland]] from Utah and [[Sandra Day O'Connor]] and [[William Rehnquist]] from Arizona}} have ever hailed from states admitted after or during the [[American Civil War|Civil War]]. Nineteen states have never produced a Supreme Court justice. In order of [[admission to the Union]] these are: {{div col|colwidth=18em}} # [[Delaware]] (original state) # [[Rhode Island]] (original state) # [[Vermont]] (admitted in 1791) # [[Arkansas]] (admitted in 1836){{efn|President Nixon reportedly intended to nominate [[Herschel Friday]] of Arkansas to a seat on the court in 1971, but changed his mind hours before announcing a different nominee.{{Cite book |last=Margolick |first=David |url=https://archive.org/details/atbarpassions00marg/page/212 |title=At the bar : the passions and peccadilloes of American lawyers |date=1995 |publisher=New York : Simon & Schuster |isbn=978-0-671-88787-2 |pages=213–4}}}} # [[Florida]] (admitted in 1845){{efn|An unsuccessful nominee, [[G. Harrold Carswell]], was from Florida. A successful nominee, [[Ketanji Brown Jackson]], was born in Washington, D.C., and appointed from there, but spent most of her childhood in Florida.}} # [[Wisconsin]] (admitted in 1848){{efn|President George W. Bush considered appointing [[Diane S. Sykes]], a Federal judge from Wisconsin, to the Supreme Court in 2005.}} # [[Oregon]] (admitted in 1859){{efn|An unsuccessful nominee, [[George Henry Williams]], was from Oregon.}} # [[West Virginia]] (admitted in 1863){{efn|West Virginia could be argued to have produced no Supreme Court justices back to the inaugural Court – it was part of Virginia between 1788 and 1863, and none of Virginia's five antebellum Supreme Court justices hailed from what became West Virginia.}} # [[Nevada]] (admitted in 1864) # [[Nebraska]] (admitted in 1867) # [[North Dakota]] (admitted in 1889) # [[South Dakota]] (admitted in 1889) # [[Montana]] (admitted in 1889){{efn|Barack Obama considered appointing [[Sidney R. Thomas]], a Federal judge from Montana, to the Supreme Court in 2010}} # [[Washington (state)]] (admitted in 1889) # [[Idaho]] (admitted in 1890) # [[Oklahoma]] (admitted in 1907) # [[New Mexico]] (admitted in 1912) # [[Alaska]] (admitted in 1959) # [[Hawaii]] (admitted in 1959) {{div col end}} ===Foreign birth=== Six justices were born outside the United States. These included [[James Wilson (Founding Father)|James Wilson]] (1789–1798), born in [[Ceres, Fife]], [[Scotland]]; [[James Iredell]] (1790–1799), born in [[Lewes]], England; and [[William Paterson (judge)|William Paterson]] (1793–1806), born in [[County Antrim]], then in the [[Kingdom of Ireland]]. Justice [[David J. Brewer]] (1889–1910) was born farthest from the U.S., in [[Smyrna]], in the [[Ottoman Empire]], (now [[İzmir]], [[Turkey]]), where his parents were American missionaries at the time.{{cite journal|last1=McAllister|first1=Stephen R.|title=The Kansas Justice, David Josiah Brewer|journal=[[The Green Bag (1997)|The Green Bag]]|date=Autumn 2015|volume=19|issue=1|page=37|url=http://www.greenbag.org/v19n1/v19n1_articles_mcallister.pdf|access-date=June 18, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161219111550/http://www.greenbag.org/v19n1/v19n1_articles_mcallister.pdf|archive-date=December 19, 2016|url-status=live}} [[George Sutherland]] (1922–1939) was born in [[Buckinghamshire]], England. The last foreign-born justice, and the only one of these for whom English was a second language, was [[Felix Frankfurter]] (1939–1962), born in [[Vienna]], [[Austria-Hungary]] (now in [[Austria]]).{{cite web|title=Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)|url=https://www.supremecourt.gov/faq_justices.aspx#faqjustice12|publisher=Supreme Court of the United States|access-date=May 3, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170320120356/https://www.supremecourt.gov/faq_justices.aspx#faqjustice12|archive-date=March 20, 2017|url-status=dead}}Kermit Hall, James W. Ely, Joel B. Grossman, ''The Oxford Companion to the Supreme Court of the United States'' (2005), p. 710; all other foreign born justices were born in English-speaking countries, except Brewer, who moved from Turkey to the United States while still in his infancy. The Constitution imposes no [[United States nationality law|citizenship]] requirement on federal judges,{{cite web |title=Frequently Asked Questions: General Information – Supreme Court of the United States |url=https://www.supremecourt.gov/about/faq_general.aspx |website=www.supremecourt.gov}} however Federal [[Appropriation (law)|appropriation law]] does require that anyone serving on the Federal judiciary be a U.S. citizen, or a lawful permanent resident who has immediately sought to acquire citizenship.{{cite web |title=Citizenship Requirements for Employment in the Judiciary {{!}} United States Courts |url=https://www.uscourts.gov/careers/search-judiciary-jobs/citizenship-requirements-employment-judiciary |website=www.uscourts.gov |language=en}} ==Ethnicity== All Supreme Court justices were [[White Americans|white]] and of mostly [[Northwestern Europe]]an heritage until the appointment of [[Thurgood Marshall]], the first African-American Justice, in 1967. Since then, only three other non-white justices have been appointed: Marshall's African-American successor, [[Clarence Thomas]], in 1991, Latina Justice [[Sonia Sotomayor]] in 2009, and African-American [[Ketanji Brown Jackson]] in 2022.{{cite book |last1=McMahon |first1=Kevin J. |title=A Supreme Court Unlike Any Other: The Deepening Divide Between the Justices and the People |date=12 April 2024 |publisher=University of Chicago Press |isbn=978-0-226-83107-7 |page=114 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Eg_tEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA114 |language=en}} {| class="wikitable sortable collapsible plainrowheaders" border="1" |+ Non-white justices !scope="col"|Name !scope="col"|Appointed

There have been several justices of [[Irish-American|Irish]] or [[Scotch-Irish American|Ulster Scots]] descent, with [[William Paterson (judge)|William Paterson]] born in Ireland to an [[Ulster Scots people|Ulster Scots]] Protestant family and [[Joseph McKenna]], [[Edward Douglas White]], [[Pierce Butler (justice)|Pierce Butler]], [[Frank Murphy]], [[William J. Brennan Jr.]], [[Anthony Kennedy]], and [[Brett Kavanaugh]] being of [[Irish Catholic]] origin. There have been five justices of [[French Americans|French]] ancestry in [[John Jay]], [[Gabriel Duval]], [[Lucius Quintus Cincinnatus Lamar]], [[Joseph Rucker Lamar]]Schmidhauser, John Richard; 'The Justices of the Supreme Court: A Collective Portrait'; ''[[Midwest Journal of Political Science]]''; vol. 3, no. 1 (February 1959), pp. 1–57. and [[Amy Coney Barrett]], with all except the Catholic Barrett being [[Protestantism in the United States|Protestants]] of [[Huguenot]] origins. Many justices – including John Jay, [[William Johnson (judge)|William Johnson]], and [[Willis Van Devanter]] – have been of [[Dutch Americans|Dutch]] Protestant origin, while two Protestant [[Scandinavian Americans]] to serve on the court have been [[Chief Justice of the United States|Chief Justices]] [[Earl Warren]] and [[William Rehnquist]].{{cite book |last1=Lago |first1=Don |title=On the Viking Trail: Travels in Scandinavian America |date=April 2004 |publisher=University of Iowa Press |isbn=978-1-58729-483-9 |page=152 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=o4urkK_1W7cC&pg=PA152 |language=en}} Up until the 1980s, only eight justices of "central, eastern, or southern European derivation" had been appointed, and even among these justices, five of them "were of Germanic background, which includes Austrian, German-Bohemian, and Swiss origins ([[John Catron]], [[Samuel Freeman Miller|Samuel F. Miller]], [[Louis Brandeis]], [[Felix Frankfurter]], and [[Warren Burger]])", with Brandeis and Frankfurter being of Ashkenazi Jewish descent, while only one justice was of non-Germanic, Southern European descent ([[Benjamin N. Cardozo]], of [[Sephardic Jewish]] descent).Schmidhauser, John Richard; ''Judges and justices: the Federal Appellate Judiciary'' (1979), p. 60. Cardozo, appointed to the court in 1932, was the first justice who did not have a Northwestern European background.{{cite book |last1=Barton |first1=Benjamin H. |title=The Credentialed Court: Inside the Cloistered, Elite Supreme Court |date=8 March 2022 |publisher=Encounter Books |isbn=978-1-64177-205-1 |pages=230–231 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aAgqEAAAQBAJ&pg=PT230 |language=en}} Both of Justice Cardozo's parents descended from [[Sephardi Jews|Sephardic Jews]] from the Iberian Peninsula who fled to Holland during the [[Spanish Inquisition]], then to London, before arriving in New York prior to the American Revolution.{{cite book|last1=Kaufman|first1=Andrew L.|title=Cardozo|date=1998|publisher=Harvard University Press|location=Cambridge, MA|isbn=978-0-674-09645-5|edition=First|chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/cardozo00kauf|access-date=June 18, 2017|chapter=1. Cardozo's Heritage: The Sephardim and Tammany Hall|page=6|quote=The family into which Benjamin Nathan Cardozo was born ... was a Sephardic family, descended from those Jews who had fled from the Iberian peninsula during the Inquisition and had come to America via the Netherlands and England. Both branches of the family (the Cardozos and the Nathans) had arrived in the American colonies before the American Revolution. Cardozo family tradition holds that their ancestors were Portuguese Marranos—Jews who practiced Judaism secretly after forced conversion to Christianity—who fled the Inquisition in the seventeenth century. They took refuge first in Holland and then in London. Later members of the family emigrated to the New World. Aaron Cardozo, was the first Cardozo to settle in the American colonies, arriving in New York from London in 1752.|via=The New York Times|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/cardozo00kauf}} At least two, [[Abe Fortas]] and [[Arthur Goldberg]], were of Eastern European Ashkenazi descent.{{cite book | last1=Maisel | first1=S.L. | last2=Forman | first2=I.N. | last3=Antler | first3=J. | last4=Burt | first4=R.A. | last5=Chanes | first5=J.A. | last6=Dalin | first6=D.G. | last7=Ginsberg | first7=B. | last8=Greenberg | first8=A. | last9=Kerbel | first9=M.R. | last10=Lieberman | first10=J.I. | title=Jews in American Politics: Essays | publisher=Rowman & Littlefield Publishers | year=2003 | isbn=978-1-4617-0462-1 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HcW4AQAAQBAJ&pg=PA73 | access-date=2024-09-22 | page=73}} Justice [[Antonin Scalia]], who served from 1986 to 2016, and Justice [[Samuel Alito]], who has served since 2006, are the first justices of Italian descent to be appointed to the Supreme Court. Justice Scalia's father and both maternal grandparents as well as both of Justice Alito's parents were born in Italy.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6e_wGCV10zIC&pg=PA185|title=American Original: The Life and Constitution of Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia|author-link=Joan Biskupic|first=Joan|last=Biskupic|date=November 10, 2009|publisher=Macmillan|isbn=9780374202897|via=Google Books|access-date=June 18, 2017|archive-date=February 22, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170222102056/https://books.google.com/books?id=6e_wGCV10zIC&pg=PA185|url-status=live}}{{cite web|last1=Walthr|first1=Matthew|title=Sam Alito: A Civil Man|url=https://spectator.org/58731_sam-alito-civil-man/|website=The American Spectator|access-date=June 15, 2017|date=April 21, 2014|via=The ANNOTICO Reports|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170522135245/https://spectator.org/58731_sam-alito-civil-man/|archive-date=May 22, 2017|url-status=dead}}{{cite news|last1=DeMarco|first1=Megan|title=Growing up Italian in Jersey: Alito reflects on ethnic heritage|url=http://www.italystl.com/ra/3788.htm|access-date=June 15, 2017|work=The Times of Trenton, New Jersey|date=February 14, 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170730160055/http://www.italystl.com/ra/3788.htm|archive-date=July 30, 2017|url-status=dead}} Justice [[Ruth Bader Ginsburg]] was born to a Jewish father who immigrated from Russia at age 13 and a Jewish mother who was born four months after her parents immigrated from Poland.{{cite web|last1=Halberstam|first1=Malvina|title=Ruth Bader Ginsburg|url=https://jwa.org/encyclopedia/article/ginsburg-ruth-bader|website=Jewish Women: A Comprehensive Historical Encyclopedia|publisher=Jewish Women's Archive|access-date=June 15, 2017|date=March 1, 2009|archive-date=March 11, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170311101214/https://jwa.org/encyclopedia/article/ginsburg-ruth-bader|url-status=live}} Among white ethnicities, according to 1959 and 1979 articles by Schmidhauser, there had never been a Justice with any [[Slavic people|Slavic]] ancestry. That changed in 2005 with the appointment of [[John Roberts]], whose mother was of Slovak ancestry.{{cite book|first1=Biskupic|last1=Joan|year=2019|title=The Chief: The Life and Turbulent Times of Chief Justice John Roberts|location=New York|publisher=Basic Books|isbn=9780465093274}} ===African-American justices=== {{see also|List of African-American jurists}} [[File:LBJ Marshall-close.jpg|thumb|[[Thurgood Marshall]], the first African-American Justice, speaking with his appointing President, [[Lyndon B. Johnson]]]] No African-American candidate was given serious consideration for appointment to the Supreme Court until the election of [[John F. Kennedy]], who weighed the possibility of appointing [[William H. Hastie]] of the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit]].Sheldon Goldman, ''Picking Federal Judges: Lower Court Selection from Roosevelt Through Reagan'' (1999), p. 184-85. {{ISBN|978-0-300-08073-5}} Hastie had been the first African-American elevated to a Court of Appeals when [[Harry S. Truman]] had so appointed him in 1949, and by the time of the Kennedy Administration, it was widely anticipated that Hastie might be appointed to the Supreme Court."What Negroes can expect from Kennedy", ''[[Ebony Magazine]]''(Jan 1961), v. 16, no. 3, p. 33. Kennedy gave serious consideration to this appointment, ensuring that this "represented the first time in American history that an African American was an actual contender for the high court". The first African-American appointed to the court was [[Thurgood Marshall]], appointed by [[Lyndon B. Johnson]] in 1967. Johnson appointed Marshall to the Supreme Court following the retirement of Justice [[Tom C. Clark]], saying that this was "the right thing to do, the right time to do it, the right man and the right place." Marshall was [[Nomination and confirmation to the Supreme Court of the United States|confirmed]] as an Associate Justice by a [[United States Senate|Senate]] vote of 69–11 on August 31, 1967.Graham, Fred P. (August 31, 1967) [https://www.nytimes.com/1967/08/31/archives/senate-confirms-marshall-as-the-first-negro-justice-10-southerners.html ''Senate Confirms Marshall As the First Negro Justice; 10 Southerners Oppose High Court Nominee in 69-to-11 Vote''.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180614123159/https://www.nytimes.com/1967/08/31/archives/senate-confirms-marshall-as-the-first-negro-justice-10-southerners.html |date=June 14, 2018 }} ''[[The New York Times]]''. Johnson confidently predicted to one biographer, [[Doris Kearns Goodwin]], that a lot of black baby boys would be named "Thurgood" in honor of this choice (in fact, Kearns's research of birth records in New York and Boston indicates that Johnson's prophecy did not come true).{{efn|According to the [[Social Security Administration]] [http://www.ssa.gov/OACT/babynames/index.html Popular baby name database], Thurgood has never been in the top 1,000 of male baby names.}} The second was [[Clarence Thomas]], appointed [[George H. W. Bush Supreme Court candidates|by George H. W. Bush]] to succeed Marshall in 1991. Bush initially wanted to nominate Thomas to replace [[William J. Brennan, Jr.|William Brennan]], who stepped down in 1990, but Bush decided that Thomas had not yet had enough experience as a judge after only months on the federal bench.{{cite news|author=Jan Crawford Greenburg|date=September 30, 2007|title=Clarence Thomas: A Silent Justice Speaks Out|work=[[ABC News (United States)|ABC News]]|url=https://abcnews.go.com/TheLaw/story?id=3664944&page=1|access-date=October 18, 2008|archive-date=September 19, 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080919015232/http://www.abcnews.go.com/TheLaw/story?id=3664944&page=1|url-status=live}} Bush nominated New Hampshire Supreme Court judge [[David Souter]] (who was of Scottish ancestry) instead. When Marshall retired for health reasons in 1991, Bush nominated a new African American justice: Clarence Thomas.{{cite news | last1=Yang | first1=John E. | last2=LaFraniere | first2=Sharon | Some historians contend that Cardozo – a [[Sephardic Jew]] whose grandfather is believed to be of distant [[Portuguese people|Portuguese]] descent{{cite web| title = Distinguished Americans & Canadians of Portuguese Descent| url= http://www.portuguesefoundation.org/famous.htm |access-date =January 9, 2008|archive-url =https://web.archive.org/web/20071212161136/http://www.portuguesefoundation.org/famous.htm |archive-date =December 12, 2007}} – should also be counted as the first [[Hispanic]] Justice. Schmidhauser wrote in 1979 that "among the large ethnic groupings of European origin which have never been represented upon the Supreme Court are the Italians, Southern Slavs, and Hispanic Americans." The National Hispanic Center for Advanced Studies and Policy Analysis wrote in 1982 that the Supreme Court "has never had an Hispanic Justice",National Hispanic Center for Advanced Studies and Policy Analysis (U.S.), ''The State of Hispanic America'' (1982), p. 98. and the ''Hispanic American Almanac'' similarly reported in 1996 that "no Hispanic has yet sat on the U.S. Supreme Court".Nicolás Kanellos, ''The Hispanic American Almanac'' (1996), p. 302. However, Segal and Spaeth state: "Though it is often claimed that no Hispanics have served on the Court, it is not clear why Benjamin Cardozo, a Sephardic Jew of Spanish heritage, should not count." They identify a number of other sources that present conflicting views as to Cardozo's ethnicity, with one simply labeling him "Iberian." In 2007, the ''Dictionary of Latino Civil Rights History'' also listed Cardozo as "the first Hispanic named to the Supreme Court of the United States."F. Arturo Rosales, ''The Dictionary of Latino Civil Rights History'', Arte Publico Press (February 28, 2007). p 59. The nomination of [[Sonia Sotomayor]], widely described in media accounts as the first Hispanic nominee, drew more attention to the question of Cardozo's ethnicity.{{Cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/05/27/us/27hispanic.html|title=Was a Hispanic Justice on the Court in the '30s?|author1-first=Neil A.|author1-last=Lewis|date=May 27, 2009|website=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=February 7, 2017|archive-date=June 30, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120630005302/http://www.nytimes.com/2009/05/27/us/27hispanic.html|url-status=live}}[https://www.usnews.com/blogs/robert-schlesinger/2009/05/26/would-sotomayor-be-the-first-hispanic-supreme-court-justice-or-was-it-cardozo.html Robert Schlesinger, ''Would Sotomayor be the First Hispanic Supreme Court Justice or Was it Cardozo?'' US News & World Report May 29, 2009] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090529010636/http://www.usnews.com/blogs/robert-schlesinger/2009/05/26/would-sotomayor-be-the-first-hispanic-supreme-court-justice-or-was-it-cardozo.html |date=May 29, 2009}} Cardozo biographer Andrew Kaufman questioned the usage of the term "hispanic" during Cardozo's lifetime, commenting: "Well, I think he regarded himself as Sephardic Jew whose ancestors came from the Iberian Peninsula." However, "no one has ever firmly established that the family's roots were, in fact, in Portugal".{{cite web|first=Mark|last=Sherman|url=http://www.foxnews.com/wires/2009May26/0,4670,USSupremeCourtFirstHispanic,00.html|title=First Hispanic justice? Some say it was Cardozo|publisher=[[Fox News]]|date=May 26, 2009|access-date=August 8, 2009|archive-date=October 23, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121023042807/http://www.foxnews.com/wires/2009May26/0,4670,USSupremeCourtFirstHispanic,00.html|url-status=live}} It has also been asserted that Cardozo himself "confessed in 1937 that his family preserved neither the Spanish language nor Iberian cultural traditions".Aviva Ben-Ur, ''Sephardic Jews in America: A Diasporic History'' (2009), p. 86. By contrast, Cardozo made his own translations of authoritative legal works written in French and German.[[Richard Polenberg]], ''The World of Benjamin Cardozo: Personal Values and the Judicial Process'' (1999), p. 88. ===Asian and other ethnic groups=== {{see also|List of Asian American jurists}} Asian-American jurists are poorly represented in the federal judicial system, and there has never been a Supreme Court justice of Asian background. According to a 2019 report of the Center for American Progress,{{cite news|title=Asian American Judges in the Federal Judiciary: A Series of Fact Sheets on the Lack of Diversity on the Bench|date=|last=Root |first=Danielle |work=Center for American Progress|url=https://americanprogress.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/JudicialDiversityFactsheet-AsianAm-4-1.pdf|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20211224172528/https://americanprogress.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/JudicialDiversityFactsheet-AsianAm-4-1.pdf|archivedate=2021-12-24}} Full report: {{cite news|title=Building a More Inclusive Federal Judiciary|date=2019|first1= Danielle|last1= Root|first2=Jake|last2= Faleschini|first3=Grace|last3= Oyenubi |work=Center for American Progress|url=https://americanprogress.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/JudicialDiversity-report-3.pdf|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20220308142145/https://americanprogress.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/JudicialDiversity-report-3.pdf|archivedate=2022-03-08}} among active federal judges serving on U.S. courts of appeals, 10 were Asian-Americans, equal to the proportion as in the overall U.S. population (5.7 percent). A 2017 study by California Justice [[Goodwin Liu]] found that of the 94 U.S. attorneys, only three were Asian American; and only 4 of the 2,437 elected prosecutors were Asian American.{{cite news|title=A Portrait of Asian Americans in the Law|date=2017|first1=Eric |last1=Chung |first2=Samuel|last2=Dong|first3=Xiaonan April|last3=Hu|first4=Christine|last4=Kwon|first5=Goodwin |last5=Liu|publisher=Yale Law School and National Asian Pacific American Bar Association|url=http://www.aapa-ca.com/assets/portrait-project_final-report.pdf|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20220626074005/http://www.aapa-ca.com/assets/portrait-project_final-report.pdf|archivedate=2022-06-26}}{{cite news|title=Law schools are filled with Asian Americans. For example, in two polls taken in 1991, one resulted in half of respondents agreeing that it was "important that there always be at least one black person" on the court while the other had only 20 percent agreeing with that sentiment, and with 77 percent agreeing that "race should never be a factor in choosing Supreme Court justices". ==Gender== [[File:President Ronald Reagan and His Supreme Court Justice Nominee Sandra Day O'Connor at The White House - DPLA - 72f7cb93bee35724d372dfa4dfde1ebe.jpg|thumb|right|[[Sandra Day O'Connor]], the first female justice, with President [[Ronald Reagan]], who appointed her]] [[File:O'Connor, Sotomayor, Ginsburg, and Kagan.jpg|thumb|right|The first four women who served on the court. From left to right: Justices [[Sandra Day O'Connor]] (ret.), [[Sonia Sotomayor]], [[Ruth Bader Ginsburg]], and [[Elena Kagan]]. October 1, 2010, prior to Justice Kagan's investiture ceremony.]] Of the 116 justices, 110 (94.8 percent) have been men. All Supreme Court justices were males until 1981, when [[Ronald Reagan]] fulfilled his [[1980 United States presidential election|1980 campaign promise]] to place a woman on the court,{{cite book|last=[[#OBrien2003|O'Brien]] |title=Storm Center|year=2003|page=53}} which he did with the appointment of [[Sandra Day O'Connor]]. O'Connor was later joined on the court by [[Ruth Bader Ginsburg]], appointed by [[Bill Clinton]] in 1993. After O'Connor retired in 2006, Ginsburg was joined by [[Sonia Sotomayor]] and [[Elena Kagan]], who were successfully appointed to the court in 2009 and 2010, respectively, by [[Barack Obama]].{{cite news |url=https://www.latimes.com/news/nationworld/nation/la-na-kagan-sworn-in-20100808,0,3379225.story |title=Elena Kagan Sworn in as Supreme Court Justice |first=Janet |last=Hook |date=August 7, 2010 |work=Los Angeles Times |access-date=August 7, 2010 |archive-date=August 11, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100811162553/http://www.latimes.com/news/nationworld/nation/la-na-kagan-sworn-in-20100808,0,3379225.story |url-status=live }} In September 2020, following Ginsburg's death, [[Donald Trump]] nominated [[Amy Coney Barrett]] to succeed her.{{cite news |author1=Steve Holland |author2=Lawrence Hurley |author3=Andrew Chung |title=Trump announces 'brilliant' conservative judge Barrett as Supreme Court pick |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-usa-court-trump/trump-announces-brilliant-conservative-judge-barrett-as-supreme-court-pick-idUSKBN26H0GI |website=reuters.com |date=September 26, 2020 |access-date=September 26, 2020 |archive-date=September 26, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200926214309/https://www.reuters.com/article/us-usa-court-trump/trump-announces-brilliant-conservative-judge-barrett-as-supreme-court-pick-idUSKBN26H0GI |url-status=live }} Barrett was confirmed the following month. Only one woman, [[Harriet Miers]], has been nominated to the court unsuccessfully. Her 2005 nomination to succeed O'Connor by [[George W. Bush]] was [[Harriet Miers Supreme Court nomination|withdrawn under fire]] from both parties, and also marked the first time when a woman was nominated to replace another woman on the court. The nomination of Barrett was the first successful nomination for a woman to succeed another woman. [[Joe Biden]]'s 2022 nomination of [[Ketanji Brown Jackson]] to a seat vacated by the retirement of [[Stephen Breyer]] makes Jackson the first African-American woman to be nominated to the court. The Senate confirmed Jackson on April 7, 2022, and she joined the court two months later. Substantial public sentiment in support of appointment of a woman to the Supreme Court has been expressed since at least as early as 1930, when an editorial in ''[[The Christian Science Monitor]]'' encouraged [[Herbert Hoover]] to consider [[Ohio Supreme Court]] Justice [[Florence E. Allen]] or assistant attorney general [[Mabel Walker Willebrandt]].{{cite book |last=[[#Maltese1998|Maltese]] |title=The Selling of Supreme Court Nominees|year=1998|page=126}} [[Franklin Delano Roosevelt]] appointed Allen to the [[United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit]] in 1934—making her "one of the highest ranking female jurists in the world at that time".{{cite book |last=[[#SalokarVolcansek1996|Salokar and Volcansek]] |title=Women in Law: A Bio-bibliographical Sourcebook |year=1996 |page=20}} However, neither Roosevelt nor his successors over the following two decades gave strong consideration to female candidates for the court. [[Harry Truman]] briefly considered appointing Allen to the Supreme Court, but was dissuaded by concerns raised by justices then serving that a woman on the court "would inhibit their conference deliberations", which were marked by informality. President [[Richard Nixon]] named [[Mildred Lillie]], then serving as a judge on the [[California Courts of Appeal|California Second District Court of Appeals]], as a potential nominee to fill one of two vacancies on the court in 1971. However, Lillie was quickly deemed unqualified by the [[American Bar Association]], and no formal proceedings were ever set with respect to her potential nomination. [[Lewis F. Powell, Jr.|Lewis Powell]] and [[William Rehnquist]] were then successfully nominated to fill those vacancies.{{cite book |last1=Johnson |first1=Hannah Brenner |last2=Jefferson |first2=Renee Knake |title=Shortlisted: Women in the Shadows of the Supreme Court |date=15 February 2022 |publisher=NYU Press |isbn=978-1-4798-1196-0 |page=44 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=a3EnEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA44 |language=en}} President [[Jimmy Carter]] seriously considered nominating former Judge [[Shirley Hufstedler]] of the [[Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals]] to the Supreme Court, but no vacancy occurred during his Presidency.{{cite book |last=Newman |first=Roger K. |date=2009 |url=https://archive.org/details/yalebiographical00newm |url-access=registration |title=The Yale Biographical Dictionary of American Law |publisher=Yale University Press |page=[https://archive.org/details/yalebiographical00newm/page/277 277] |isbn=978-0-300-11300-6}} In 1991, a poll found that 53 percent of Americans felt it "important that there always be at least one woman" on the court. Supreme Court justices have been married. [[William H. Moody]], [[Frank Murphy]], [[Benjamin Cardozo]], [[James Clark McReynolds]], and [[David Souter]] were all lifelong bachelors.{{cite news | url=http://voices.washingtonpost.com/reliable-source/2009/05/rs-sonia27.html | first1=Amy | last1=Argetsinger | first2=Roxanne | last2=Roberts | author-link1=Amy Argetsinger | author-link2=Roxanne Roberts | title=Sotomayor: A Single Supreme? | newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] | date=May 27, 2009 | access-date=July 10, 2010 | series=The Reliable Source | archive-date=June 6, 2012 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120606144014/http://voices.washingtonpost.com/reliable-source/2009/05/rs-sonia27.html | url-status=dead }} In addition, current justice [[Elena Kagan]] has never been married."[https://web.archive.org/web/20100513081527/http://www.reuters.com/article/idUSTRE64910220100510 Kagan bucks 40-year trend as court pick]", Reuters News, May 10, 2010.Lisa Belkin, "[https://www.nytimes.com/2010/05/23/magazine/23FOB-wwln-t.html Judging Women] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151116062004/http://www.nytimes.com/2010/05/23/magazine/23FOB-wwln-t.html |date=November 16, 2015 }}", ''[[The New York Times Magazine]]'' (May 18, 2010). [[William O. Douglas]] was the first Justice to divorce while on the court and also had the most marriages of any Justice, with four. Justice [[John Paul Stevens]] divorced his first wife in 1979, marrying his second wife later that year. [[Sonia Sotomayor]] was the first female justice to be appointed as an unmarried woman, having divorced in 1983, long before her nomination in 2009. Of the six women who have been appointed to the Court, O'Connor and Ginsburg were the only two military spouses.{{Cite web |last=Preston |first=Matthew |date=April 15, 2022 |title=Ketanji Brown Jackson's historic rise leaves just one military veteran on the Supreme Court |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/opinion/columnist/2022/04/15/supreme-court-ketanji-brown-jackson-veteran/9510328002/ |access-date=October 9, 2022 |website=USA Today |language=en-US}} Several justices have become widowers while on the bench. The 1792 death of Elizabeth Rutledge, wife of Justice [[John Rutledge]], contributed to the mental health problems that led to the rejection of his recess appointment.{{cite book|last=Flanders|first=Henry|title=The Lives and Times of the Chief Justices of the Supreme Court of the United States|orig-year=1874|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qbE427HiSx0C&pg=PA431|access-date=April 29, 2008|volume=1|publisher=J. B. Lippincott & Co.|location=Philadelphia|year=1874|archive-date=April 26, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160426220336/https://books.google.com/books?id=qbE427HiSx0C&pg=PA431|url-status=live}} [[Roger B. Taney]] survived his wife, Anne, by twenty years. [[Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr.]] resolutely continued working on the court for several years after the death of his wife.{{cite book|author=White, Edward G.|title= Oliver Wendell Holmes, Jr|url=https://archive.org/details/oliverwendellhol00whit|url-access=limited|year=2006|page=[https://archive.org/details/oliverwendellhol00whit/page/n141 131]|publisher= Oxford University Press, USA|isbn= 978-0-19-530536-4}} William Rehnquist was a widower for the last fourteen years of his service on the court, his wife Natalie having died on October 17, 1991, after suffering from [[ovarian cancer]]. With the death of [[Martin D. Ginsburg]] in June 2010, Ruth Bader Ginsburg became the first woman to be widowed while serving on the court.{{cite news |url=http://voices.washingtonpost.com/postmortem/2010/06/husband-of-supreme-court-justi.html |title=Husband of Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg dies |date=June 27, 2010 |newspaper=The Washington Post |access-date=June 27, 2010 |archive-date=March 4, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304094526/http://voices.washingtonpost.com/postmortem/2010/06/husband-of-supreme-court-justi.html |url-status=dead }} ===Sexual orientation=== With regards to [[sexual orientation]], there is no conclusive evidence that there has ever been an [[LGBT]] Supreme Court justice.{{cite web | last=Wegman | first=Jesse | title=What if the Supreme Court Had an L.G.B.T. Justice? | website=The New York Times | date=2019-10-12 | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/10/12/opinion/sunday/what-if-the-supreme-court-had-an-lgbt-justice.html | access-date=2024-09-22}} [[G. Harrold Carswell]] was unsuccessfully nominated by [[Richard Nixon]] in 1970 and was convicted in 1976 of [[battery (crime)|battery]] for making an "unnatural and lascivious" advance to a male police officer working undercover in a Florida men's room.{{cite book |last=[[#MurdochPrice2002|Murdoch and Price]] |title=Courting Justice: Gay Men and Lesbians V. the Supreme Court |year=2002|page= 187}} Some therefore claim him as the only gay or [[bisexual]] person nominated to the court thus far.{{cite book |first=Keith |last=Stern |title=Queers in History |year=2006|page=84}} Stating of Carswell, "He's the only known homosexual to have been nominated to the Supreme Court, though he was in the closet".{{cite book |last=[[#Dean2001|Dean]]|title=The Rehnquist Choice: The Untold Story of the Nixon Appointment That Redefined the Supreme Court |year=2001 |page=20}} If so, it is unlikely that Nixon was aware of it; [[White House Counsel]] [[John Dean]] later wrote of Carswell that "[w]hile Richard Nixon was always looking for historical firsts, nominating a homosexual to the high court would not have been on his list". Speculation has been recorded about the sexual orientation of a few justices who were lifelong bachelors, but no unambiguous evidence exists that they were gay. Perhaps the greatest body of circumstantial evidence surrounds [[Frank Murphy]], who was dogged by "rumors of homosexuality ... all his adult life".Joyce Murdoch and Deb Price, ''Courting Justice: Gay Men and Lesbians v. The Supreme Court'' (New York: Basic Books, 2001) p. 18.
For more than 40 years, Edward G. Kemp was Frank Murphy's devoted, trusted companion. Like Murphy, Kemp was a lifelong bachelor. From college until Murphy's death, the pair found creative ways to work and live together. [...] When Murphy appeared to have the better future in politics, Kemp stepped into a supportive, secondary role.Joyce Murdoch and Deb Price, ''Courting Justice: Gay Men and Lesbians v. The Supreme Court'' (New York: Basic Books, 2001) pp. 19–20.
As well as Murphy's close relationship with Kemp, Murphy's biographer, historian [[Sidney Fine (historian)|Sidney Fine]], found in Murphy's personal papers a letter that "if the words mean what they say, refers to a homosexual encounter some years earlier between Murphy and the writer." However, the letter's veracity cannot be confirmed, and a review of all the evidence led Fine to conclude that he "could not stick his neck out and say [Murphy] was gay".Quoted in Joyce Murdoch and Deb Price, ''Courting Justice: Gay Men and Lesbians v. The Supreme Court'' (New York: Basic Books, 2001) p. 19. Speculation has also surrounded [[Benjamin Cardozo]], whose [[celibate|celibacy]] was proposed to suggest repressed homosexuality or asexuality. The fact that he was unmarried and was personally tutored by the writer [[Horatio Alger, Jr.|Horatio Alger]] (alleged to have had sexual relations with boys) led some of Cardozo's biographers to insinuate that Cardozo was homosexual, but no real evidence exists to corroborate this possibility. Constitutional law scholar [[Jeffrey Rosen (legal academic)|Jeffrey Rosen]] noted in a ''[[The New York Times Book Review]]'' of [[Richard Polenberg]]'s book on Cardozo:
Polenberg describes Cardozo's lifelong devotion to his older sister Nell, with whom he lived in New York until her death in 1929. When asked why he had never married, Cardozo replied, quietly and sadly, "I never could give Nellie the second place in my life." Polenberg suggests that friends may have stressed Cardozo's devotion to his sister to discourage rumors "that he was sexually dysfunctional, or had an unusually low sexual drive or was homosexual." But he produces no evidence to support any of these possibilities, except to note that friends, in describing Cardozo, used words like "beautiful", "exquisite", "sensitive" or "delicate."{{cite news |last1=Rosen |first1=Jeffrey |title=The Hopeless Moralist |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=November 2, 1997 |url=https://archive.nytimes.com/www.nytimes.com/books/97/11/02/reviews/971102.02rosent.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151002042903/http://www.nytimes.com/books/97/11/02/reviews/971102.02rosent.html |archive-date=October 2, 2015}}
Andrew Kaufman, author of ''Cardozo'', a biography published in 2000, notes that "Although one cannot be absolutely certain, it seems highly likely that Cardozo lived a celibate life".{{cite book|last=[[#Kaufman1998|Kaufman]] |title=Cardozo|year=1998|page=68}} Judge [[Learned Hand]] is quoted in the book as saying about Cardozo: "He [had] no trace of homosexuality anyway".{{cite book |last=[[#Kaufman1998|Kaufman]] |title=Cardozo|year= 1998|pages= 68–69}} More recently, when [[David Souter]] was nominated to the court, "conservative groups expressed concern to the White House ... that the president's bachelor nominee might conceivably be a homosexual".[[Tinsley E. Yarbrough]], "David Hackett Souter: Traditional Republican on the Rehnquist Court" (Oxford University Press, 2005), p. viii. Similar questions were raised regarding the sexual orientation of unmarried nominee Elena Kagan.{{cite news | title=From softball to Bridget Jones: Why we should stop talking about Elena Kagan's sexuality | last=Baird | first=Julia | author-link=Julia Baird (journalist) | url=http://www.newsweek.com/2010/05/12/from-softball-to-bridget-jones.html | access-date=August 5, 2010 | newspaper=Newsweek | date=May 12, 2010 | archive-date=August 11, 2010 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100811193837/http://www.newsweek.com/2010/05/12/from-softball-to-bridget-jones.html | url-status=live }} However, no evidence was ever produced regarding Souter's sexual orientation, and Kagan's apparent heterosexuality was attested by colleagues familiar with her dating history.Ruth Marcus, [https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2010/05/13/AR2010051304685.html Elena Kagan: A smart woman with fewer choices?] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170403141322/http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2010/05/13/AR2010051304685.html |date=April 3, 2017 }}, ''The Washington Post'' (Friday, May 14, 2010). ==Religion== When the Supreme Court was established in 1789, the first members came from among the ranks of the [[Founding Fathers of the United States|Founding Fathers]] and were almost uniformly Protestant. Of the 116 justices who have been appointed to the court, 92 have been from various Protestant denominations and 15 have been Catholics (one other justice, [[Sherman Minton]], began practicing Catholicism after leaving the court).{{cite book|title=Sherman Minton: New Deal Senator, Cold War Justice|last1=Gugin|first1=Linda|last2=St. Clair|first2=James E.|publisher=Indiana Historical Society|year=1997|isbn=978-0-87195-116-8|page=304}} Another, [[Neil Gorsuch]], was raised in the Catholic Church but later attended an [[Episcopal Church (United States)|Episcopal]] church, though without specifying the denomination to which he felt he belonged. Eight justices have been Jewish and one, [[David Davis (Supreme Court justice)|David Davis]], had no known religious affiliation.{{Cite web|url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/more-than-2-centuries-of-supreme-court-justices-in-18-numbers|title=More than 2 centuries of Supreme Court justices, in 18 numbers|date=July 9, 2018|first1=Rachel|last1=Wellford|website=PBS NewsHour|quote=Only one justice, David Davis, had no religious affiliation.}} Three of the 17 chief justices have been Catholics, and one Jewish justice, [[Abe Fortas]], was nominated to be chief justice,{{cite report| last=McMillion| first=Barry J.| date= January 28, 2022| title=Supreme Court Nominations, 1789 to 2020: Actions by the Senate, the Judiciary Committee, and the President| url=https://sgp.fas.org/crs/misc/RL33225.pdf| publisher=Congressional Research Service| location=Washington, D.C.| access-date=February 21, 2022}} though this nomination was withdrawn in the face of a filibuster.{{cite journal|author1-link= Keith Whittington| last=Whittington| first=Keith E.| title=Presidents, Senates, and failed Supreme Court Nominations| url=https://scholar.princeton.edu/sites/default/files/failed_nominations_0.pdf| journal=Supreme Court Review| publisher=The University of Chicago Press| pages= 401–438| volume=2006| year=2006| doi=10.1086/655178| s2cid=141654668| access-date=March 10, 2022| via=scholar.princeton.edu}} {{anchor|religiontable}}The table below shows the religious affiliation of each of the justices sitting {{As of|2022|lc=on|July|df=US}}: {| class="wikitable sortable plainrowheaders" |+ Religious makeup of the current court !scope="col"|Name !scope="col"|Religion !scope="col"|Appt. by !scope="col"|On the court since |- !scope="row"|{{Sortname|John|Roberts}} ([[Chief Justice of the United States|Chief Justice]]) |Catholicism |[[George W. These have included 33 [[Episcopal Church (United States)|Episcopalians]], 18 Presbyterians, nine [[Unitarianism|Unitarians]], five [[Methodism|Methodists]], three [[Baptists]], two [[Disciples of Christ]], and lone representatives of various other denominations.{{cite web|url=http://www.adherents.com/adh_sc.html|title=Religion of the Supreme Court|publisher=adherents.com|date=March 11, 2020|url-status=usurped|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200311105236/http://www.adherents.com/adh_sc.html|archive-date=March 11, 2020}} (archived) [[William Rehnquist]] and [[William R. Day]] were the court's only [[Lutheranism|Lutherans]]. [[Noah Haynes Swayne|Noah Swayne]] was a [[Religious Society of Friends|Quaker]]. Some fifteen Protestant justices did not adhere to a particular denomination. The religious beliefs of [[James Wilson (Founding Father)|James Wilson]], one of the earliest justices, have been the subject of some dispute, as there are writings from various points of his life from which it can be argued that he leaned towards [[Presbyterianism]], [[Anglicanism]], [[Thomism]], or [[Deism]]; it has been deemed likely that he eventually favored some form of Christianity.Mark D. Hall, "James Wilson: Presbyterian, Anglican, Thomist, or Deist? Does it Matter?", in Daniel L. Dreisbach, Mark David Hall, Jeffrey Morrison, Jeffry H. Morrison, eds., ''The Founders on God and Government'' (2004). p. 181, 184–195. [[Baptist]] denominations and other [[evangelicalism|evangelical]] churches have been underrepresented on the court relative to the population of the United States, and entirely unrepresented since the retirement of Methodist [[Harry Blackmun]] in 1994. Conversely, [[mainline Protestant]] churches historically were overrepresented. Following the retirement of [[John Paul Stevens]] in June 2010, the court had an entirely non-Protestant composition for the first time in its history.[[Nina Totenberg]], "Supreme Court May Soon Lack Protestant Justices," [[NPR]], ''Heard on Morning Edition'', April 7, 2010, found at [https://www.npr.org/templates/story/story.php?storyId=125641988 NPR website] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171024233413/http://www.npr.org/templates/story/story.php?storyId=125641988 |date=October 24, 2017 }} and transcript found at [https://www.npr.org/templates/transcript/transcript.php?storyId=125641988 NPR website] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180103193416/https://www.npr.org/templates/transcript/transcript.php?storyId=125641988 |date=January 3, 2018 }}. I am Protestant...non-denominational.}} ===Catholic justices=== [[File:Roger Taney.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Roger B. Taney]], the first Catholic justice]] The first Catholic justice, [[Roger B. Taney]], was appointed chief justice in 1836 by [[Andrew Jackson]]. The second, [[Edward Douglass White]], was appointed as an associate justice in 1894, but also went on to become chief justice. [[Joseph McKenna]] was appointed in 1898, placing two Catholics on the court until White's death in 1921. This period marked the beginning of an inconsistently observed "tradition" of having a "Catholic seat" on the court.[https://web.archive.org/web/20060215105343/http://www.catholicleague.org/research/catholics_and_the_supreme_court.htm Hitchcock, James, ''Catholics and the Supreme Court: An Uneasy Relationship'' (June 2004)] (from [[Catalyst (magazine)|Catalyst]]). Other Catholic justices included [[Pierce Butler (justice)|Pierce Butler]] (appointed 1923) and [[Frank Murphy]] (appointed 1940). Justice [[James F. Byrnes]] was a lapsed Catholic.{{cite book |last1=Parker |first1=Richard |title=John Kenneth Galbraith: His Life, His Politics, His Economics |date=12 May 2015 |publisher=Macmillan + ORM |isbn=978-1-4668-9375-7 |page=165 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=AgK6BwAAQBAJ&pg=PA165 |language=en}} [[Sherman Minton]], appointed in 1949, was a Protestant during his time on the court. To some, however, his wife's Catholic faith implied a "Catholic seat".{{cite news|title=Indiana Man Is Nominated for U.S. Court Post|work=[[Kentucky New Era]]|agency=Associated Press|date=September 15, 1949|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=Ae0rAAAAIBAJ&pg=2057%2C5000964|access-date=November 29, 2020|archive-date=December 9, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201209200514/https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=Ae0rAAAAIBAJ&pg=2057,5000964|url-status=live}} Minton joined his wife's church in 1961, five years after he retired from the court.{{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20010405054827/http://www.adherents.com/adh_sc.html Religious affiliation of Supreme Court justices]}} Justice [[Sherman Minton]] converted to Catholicism after his retirement. [[James F. Byrnes]] was raised as Catholic, but became an [[Episcopal Church (United States)|Episcopalian]] before his confirmation as a Supreme Court Justice. Minton was succeeded by a Catholic, however, when President [[Dwight Eisenhower|Eisenhower]] appointed [[William J. Brennan, Jr.|William J. Brennan]] to that seat. Eisenhower sought a Catholic to appoint to the court—in part because there had been no Catholic justice since Murphy's death in 1949, and in part because Eisenhower was directly lobbied by [[Francis Spellman|Francis Cardinal Spellman]] of the [[Archdiocese of New York]] to make such an appointment.Jeffrey A. Segal, Harold J. Spaeth, ''The Supreme Court and the Attitudinal Model Revisited'' (2002) p. 184. Brennan was then the lone Catholic justice in 1985, but by the 21st century there would be six Catholic justices on the court.{{cite web |title=Sotomayor would be part of court's Catholic shift |url=https://edition.cnn.com/2009/POLITICS/05/27/sotomayor.catholic/ |website=CNN}} Like Sherman Minton, Clarence Thomas was not a Catholic at the time he was appointed to the court. Thomas was raised Catholic and briefly attended [[Conception Seminary College]], a [[Catholic Church|Catholic]] [[seminary]],[http://www.conceptionabbey.org/TowerTopics/TTWinter2001/CThomas.htm Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas visits Conception Seminary College] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080321033051/http://www.conceptionabbey.org/TowerTopics/TTWinter2001/CThomas.htm |date=March 21, 2008}}, Winter 2001. but had joined the Protestant denomination of his wife after their marriage. At some point in the late 1990s, Thomas returned to Catholicism. In 2005, [[John Roberts]] became the third Catholic Chief Justice and the fourth Catholic on the court. Shortly thereafter, [[Samuel Alito]] became the fifth on the court, and the eleventh in the history of the court. Alito's appointment gave the court a Catholic majority for the first time in its history.{{Cite web|url=https://www.ewtnnews.com/world/us/experts-ponder-catholic-majority-us-supreme-court|title=Experts ponder Catholic-majority U.S. Supreme Court|website=Catholic News Agency|date=January 31, 2006}} In contrast to historical patterns, the court has gone from having a "Catholic seat" to being what some have characterized as a "Catholic court". The reasons for that are subject to debate.{{cite web|url=http://www.press.georgetown.edu/detail.html?id=9781589012158|first1=Barbara A.|last1=Perry|author-link1=Barbara A. Perry|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100612145154/http://www.press.georgetown.edu/detail.html?id=9781589012158 |archive-date=June 12, 2010|url-status=dead|title=Catholics and the Supreme Court: From the 'Catholic Seat' to the New Majority|work=Catholics and Politics: The Dynamic Tension between Faith and Power|publisher=Georgetown University Press|date=October 2008|editor1-first=K. E. |editor1-last=Heyer |editor2-first=M. J. |editor2-last=Rozell |editor3-first=M. A. |editor3-last=Genovese}} The fact that most recent Catholic appointees were also ideologically conservative has led some partisan critics to derisively refer to the court as "a Catholic boys club".[http://www.religiondispatches.org/blog/politics/1455/catholic_boy%E2%80%99s_club:_religion_and_the_supreme_court Kissling, Frances (May 17, 2009) ''Catholic Boy's Club: Religion and the Supreme Court'' Religious Dispatches] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211030161624/https://religiondispatches.org/catholic-boys-club-religion-and-the-supreme-court/ |date=October 30, 2021 }}. Frances Kissling is a visiting scholar at the Center for Bioethics at the [[University of Pennsylvania]] and former president of [[Catholics for a Free Choice]]. However in May 2009, President [[Barack Obama]] nominated a Catholic woman, [[Sonia Sotomayor]], to replace retiring Justice [[David Souter]].[https://www.boston.com/news/local/articles_of_faith/2009/05/sotomayor_would.html Paulson, Michael''' Catholicism: Sotomayor would be sixth Catholic''' May 26, 2009.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130117064103/http://www.boston.com/news/local/articles_of_faith/2009/05/sotomayor_would.html |date=January 17, 2013 }} ''[[The Boston Globe]]''. Her confirmation raised the number of Catholics on the court to six, compared to three non-Catholics. With [[Antonin Scalia]]'s death in February 2016, the number of Catholic justices went back to five. Scalia's replacement, [[Neil Gorsuch]], appointed in 2017, was raised Catholic but attends and is a member of an Episcopal church; it is unclear if he identifies as a Catholic as well as belonging to the [[Episcopal Church (United States)|Episcopal Church]]. Following [[Anthony Kennedy]]'s retirement in July 2018, the number of Catholic justices remained unchanged as he was succeeded by Catholic [[Brett Kavanaugh]]. Benjamin]] to be the first Jewish justice, and ''[[The New York Times]]'' reported (on February 15, 1853) that "if the President nominates Benjamin, the Democrats are determined to confirm him". However, Benjamin declined the offer, and ultimately became [[Confederate States Secretary of State|Secretary of State for the Confederacy]] during the [[United States Civil War|Civil War]]. The first Jewish nominee, [[Louis Brandeis]], was appointed in 1916, after a tumultuous hearing process. The 1932 appointment of [[Benjamin N. Cardozo|Benjamin Cardozo]] raised mild controversy for placing two Jewish justices on the court at the same time, although the appointment was widely lauded based on Cardozo's qualifications, and the Senate was unanimous in confirming Cardozo.''The New York Times'', February 25, 1932, p. 1. Most Jewish Supreme Court justices were of Ashkenazi Jewish descent, with the exception of Cardozo, who was Sephardic. None of the Jewish Supreme Court justices have practiced [[Orthodox Judaism]] while on the court, although [[Abe Fortas]] was raised Orthodox.{{Cite news|url=https://www.jewishpress.com/sections/features/features-on-jewish-world/abe-fortas-and-nixons-franking-privilege/2018/10/17/|title=Abe Fortas and Nixon's 'Franking' Privilege|last=Singer|first=Saul Jay|date=October 17, 2018|work=[[The Jewish Press]]|access-date=September 18, 2019|quote=Although raised Orthodox, Fortas was himself not observant, to the point that he married a Protestant; as Professor David Dalin writes, "[F]or Fortas, his parents' Judaism was always an obstacle to be overcome rather than a heritage to be celebrated.|archive-date=February 1, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190201030912/https://www.jewishpress.com/sections/features/features-on-jewish-world/abe-fortas-and-nixons-franking-privilege/2018/10/17/|url-status=live}} Cardozo was succeeded by another Jewish justice, [[Felix Frankfurter]], but Brandeis was succeeded by Protestant [[William O. Douglas]]. Negative reaction to the appointment of the early Jewish justices did not exclusively come from outside the court. Justice [[James Clark McReynolds]], a blatant [[anti-semite]], refused to speak to Brandeis for three years following the latter's appointment and when Brandeis retired in 1939, did not sign the customary dedicatory letter sent to court members on their retirement. During [[Benjamin N. Cardozo|Benjamin Cardozo's]] swearing in ceremony McReynolds pointedly read a newspaper muttering "another one" and did not attend that of Frankfurter, exclaiming "My God, another Jew on the Court!"Henry Julian Abraham, ''Justices, Presidents, and Senators: A History of the U.S. Supreme Court Appointments from Washington to Bush II'' (2007), p. 140. Frankfurter was followed by [[Arthur Goldberg]] and [[Abe Fortas]], each of whom filled what became known as the "Jewish seat".{{cite web| title=The 'Jewish Seat' On The Supreme Court| date=May 28, 2009 |last=Rudin| first=Ken| url=https://www.npr.org/sections/politicaljunkie/2009/05/heres_a_question_from_carol.html| publisher=[[NPR]]| access-date=February 22, 2022}} After Fortas resigned in 1969, he was replaced by Protestant [[Harry Blackmun]]. No Jewish justices were nominated thereafter until Ronald Reagan nominated [[Douglas H. Ginsburg]] in 1987, to fill the vacancy created by the retirement of [[Lewis F. Powell]]; however, this nomination was withdrawn, and the court remained without any Jewish justices until 1993, when [[Ruth Bader Ginsburg]] (unrelated to Douglas Ginsburg) was appointed to replace [[Byron White]]. Ginsburg was followed in relatively quick succession by the appointment of [[Stephen Breyer]], also Jewish, in 1994 to replace Blackmun. In 2010, the confirmation of President Barack Obama's nomination of Elena Kagan to the court created the possibility that three Jewish justices would serve simultaneously. Prior to this confirmation, [[Conservatism in the United States|conservative]] political commentator [[Pat Buchanan]] stated that, "If Kagan is confirmed, Jews, who represent less than 2 percent of the U.S. population, will have 33 percent of the Supreme Court seats".{{cite magazine|url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/pat-buchanan-msnbc-leaves-292073|title=Pat Buchanan Officially Out at MSNBC|date=February 16, 2012|first=Marisa|last=Guthrie|magazine=[[The Hollywood Reporter]]|access-date=November 10, 2019|archive-date=November 10, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191110210315/https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/pat-buchanan-msnbc-leaves-292073|url-status=live}} At the time of his remarks, 6.4 percent of justices in the history of the court had been Jewish. Justice Ginsburg died in 2020, leaving only two Jews on the Supreme Court: Breyer and Kagan. Breyer announced his retirement in 2022, which left Kagan as the only Jew on the Court.{{cite web |last1=Deutch |first1=Gabby |title=Breyer retirement leaves open the Court's 'Jewish seat' |url=https://jewishinsider.com/2022/01/breyer-retirement-leaves-open-the-courts-jewish-seat/ |website=Jewish Insider |date=27 January 2022}} {| class="wikitable sortable collapsible plainrowheaders" border="1" |+ Jewish justices !scope="col"|Name !scope="col"|Appointed
